The first trap that turns a "research only" label into a federal target is hiding in plain sight at checkout.

It's not the compound. It's what you put next to it.

🧵 A thread on kitting, cross-selling, and the FDA's Objective Intent Doctrine:

---

The FDA does not need your marketing copy to convict you.

Under 21 CFR 201.128, "intended use" is established by the objective characteristics of the product itself — not by the disclaimer you wrote at the bottom of the page.

A "research only" label is one data point. The FDA weighs all of them.

---

Specific example.

Listing BPC-157 or TB-500 on the same product page or cart as:
— bacteriostatic water
— insulin syringes
— 29–31 gauge injection supplies

…is treated as evidence of intended subcutaneous delivery to humans.

The "research only" sticker doesn't override what the cart shows.

---

This isn't theoretical.

In March 2023 the FDA issued a Warning Letter to Grand Health Inc. (doing business as "Gram Peptides") for selling tirzepatide and retatrutide alongside bacteriostatic water and related supplies.

The agency cited the integrated offering as proof of intended human use.

---

The Warning Letter is public. Anyone can read it.

What the FDA actually wrote: when the product is sold as part of a kit that includes reconstitution supplies, the whole offering is treated as an unapproved new drug — not as a research reagent.

Disclaimers were present on the site. They did not protect the company.

---

This is the trap.

Most creators think: "I added 'not for human use' — I'm covered."

The FDA reads: kitting + supplies + therapeutic keywords + pricing in human-relevant units = intended use.

The label is one input. The whole operation is the evidence.

---

When my own terrain was destroyed, the only path I trusted was board-certified physicians and 503A compounding pharmacies.

That separation isn't optional. It's the difference between a research supply shop and an unapproved new drug operation in the FDA's eyes.

content:
You can keep your public copy technically perfect and still get hit — because the FDA reads your backend.

The trap most creators never think to audit:

🧵 SEO, metadata, alt text, URL slugs, schema. The signals the FDA actually crawls:

---

Disclaimers live on the page you wrote.

The FDA reads: alt text on your product images. URL slugs on your blog posts. Schema markup behind the scenes. Meta descriptions that auto-populate when someone shares your link.

The "research only" copy on your homepage is one input. The backend is the rest.

---

Concrete examples the agency treats as evidence of intended use:

— Bidding on or ranking for "BPC-157 for gut healing"
— URL slug: /peptides-for-anxiety/
— Alt text on a vial image: "BPC-157 injection for connective tissue repair"
— Meta description: "Compounded BPC-157 for tendon recovery."

These are the signals regulators crawl first.

---

Schema is the easy miss.

If your product page emits `Product` schema with claims like "treatment for X," "effective for Y," or therapeutic keywords in the description field — search engines and regulators both see that.

The JSON-LD sits in your source. It's not a hidden field. It's public.

---

This is why "we never claimed it was for humans" stops working the moment your SEO or schema does.

The Objective Intent Doctrine (21 CFR 201.128) weighs the whole operation. The FDA doesn't accept "our developer made a typo" as a defense for a /peptides-for-anxiety slug.

---

Audit yourself before someone else does.

Three checks you can run today:
1. Pull every image alt text on product pages.
2. Grep your URL slugs for therapeutic keywords.
3. View source on product pages and read the JSON-LD.

Anything that reads as a clinical claim is a future warning letter.

---

"My body, not yours" close:

The reason I built this brand on proof over claims is exactly this. The data layer — biomarkers, scans, my own symptom log — survives any audit.

What I track in my own body is mine to publish. What I claim a compound does in yours is a federal case waiting to happen.

One comment can turn your entire page into misbranded drug labeling under Section 505(a).

The third trap most modern creators walk into blind:

🧵 Un-redacted testimonials, community claims, and why hosting adopts them as yours:

---

Section 505(a) defines a misbranded drug in part by its labeling.

"Labeling" isn't just the bottle. It's every statement that accompanies the product — website copy, ads, AND content you host or feature.

If a comment claims "[compound] healed my [condition]" and you leave it up, the FDA can treat that as your labeling.

---

This applies even when:
— the comment is in a private community you moderate
— the testimonial is on a third-party review site you link to
— the user wrote it without you asking
— you put a "results not typical" disclaimer above the comments section

Hosting adopts.

---

The practical rule:

Delete. Or heavily qualify.

"Delete" means remove the comment, screenshot it for your records, and document why you deleted it.

"Heavily qualify" means visibly mark it as third-party experience, not your product's claim — and even then, the FDA can still push back.

---

There is no middle ground of "well they wrote it, not me."

The FDA's framing: you built the venue. You curate the venue. You profit from the venue. The user-generated content in your venue is part of your labeling.

The legal exposure flows to you.

---

This is why I rebuilt the Dose of Proof site last week.

Every "verified member" testimonial that named a specific compound or claimed a specific outcome got deleted or rewritten. The product data that mentioned "sourcing links" or "exact dosing protocols" got reframed to research education only.

The model has to match the message.

---

"My body, not yours" close:

This is the rule that keeps me clean: every story I tell is mine.

My HRV. My TyTron scans. My flushing episodes. My own data, from my own body, in my own words.

The moment you start extrapolating other people's outcomes to a compound, you are no longer telling a story. You are making a claim.

The fourth trap is the one most modern creators walk into with their eyes open.

It's not a single product page. It's the architecture around it.

🧵 Why "education" + "community" + "storefront" in the same ecosystem is the pattern the FDA reads as a single drug operation:

---

Setup:

You run a Substack or YouTube channel about peptides. Educational. Compliant language. Top of funnel.

You run a Skool or Discord community. Members discuss dosing, sourcing, side effects.

You link the community from your content. Members know where to buy.

You don't sell anything yourself. You don't link your storefront.

That still reads as integrated.

---

The FDA's framing:

— Educational content that drives traffic to a community
— Community that hosts dosing discussion + sourcing referrals
— Operator that profits from the community (paid tier, affiliate revenue, brand deals)

= A single integrated marketing operation for an unapproved drug.

---

Moderation isn't the defense it sounds like.

Removing a single dosing thread after-the-fact doesn't undo the ecosystem pattern. The agency weighs:
— how the community is positioned
— what topics recur
— whether operators curate or just remove the worst offenders
— whether the operator profits from the community's existence

---

The architecture of the trap:

Education (top of funnel) → Community (engagement + retention) → Affiliate or storefront (monetization)

This is the standard creator economy stack. It is also the exact pattern the FDA reads as integrated marketing of an unapproved new drug when the topic is research-restricted compounds.

---

The separation rule:

The brand operator's money and the brand operator's editorial content must be clearly separated from any dosing, sourcing, or efficacy discussion.

That means: no community you operate. No Discord you moderate. No Skool with paid tiers where dosing is discussed. No affiliate link to a vendor inside the same ecosystem as your educational content.

Or it means: very strict separation, with legal review.

---

This is the architectural reason Dose of Proof has no integrated community. Yet.

The plan: Skool launches AFTER the July 23-24 PCAC decision window, with explicit topic boundaries (no dosing discussion in the community; physician-only dosing conversations happen elsewhere). Until then, the only community surface is the Substack comment thread — moderated, single-layer, no paid tier.

Architecture before content. Always.

On July 23 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee evaluates BPC-157 — free base and acetate forms — specifically for the ulcerative colitis indication.

Most of what you'll read this month is noise. Here's the actual regulatory record:

🧵 BPC-157 going into the July 23 PCAC:

---

Background.

BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid synthetic peptide derived from human gastric juice. It has been studied in animal models for angiogenic, regenerative, and anti-inflammatory effects.

It is NOT an FDA-approved drug for any indication. It is not in Category 1 (which would permit compounding). It has been a Category 2 bulk substance since 2023.

---

What Category 2 actually means:

— Cannot be used as a bulk substance in compounding under Section 503A
— "Significant safety risks" — the FDA's language
— Specifically cited for BPC-157: immunogenicity risk + insufficient API characterization + impurity profile unclear

These are manufacturing + safety concerns, not efficacy findings.

---

In April 2026 the FDA REMOVED BPC-157 from the Category 2 list.

That's a meaningful procedural change. It doesn't approve the compound. It opens the door for the PCAC to formally evaluate it for inclusion on the 503A Bulks List.

The July 23 meeting is that evaluation.

---

What the committee actually does on July 23:

The PCAC reviews clinical and safety data for nominated bulk substances and votes on whether to recommend inclusion on the 503A Bulks List.

A "yes" vote is a recommendation. It is NOT a final FDA decision. The FDA then considers the recommendation and issues its own determination — sometimes months later.

---

What a positive recommendation would change:

— State-licensed 503A compounding pharmacies could theoretically prepare BPC-157 formulations for individual patients with valid prescriptions
— Physicians could prescribe it within the compounding pathway
— Telehealth platforms partnered with 503A pharmacies (Marek Health, Lifeforce) could offer it under physician oversight

This is physician-supervised only. Not direct-to-consumer.

---

What a positive recommendation would NOT change:

— BPC-157 would still not be FDA-approved for any indication
— Manufacturers could not sell it direct-to-consumer
— "Research only" marketing that names human therapeutic uses would still violate 21 CFR 201.128
— Sourcing from gray-market vendors would still be illegal

The map changes the legal pathway. It does not change the underlying architecture.

---

"My body, not yours" close:

When my own gut was wrecked from mold exposure, I did not self-experiment with raw powders. I went through board-certified physicians, asked about 503A compounding eligibility, and only considered peptides that had a defensible regulatory pathway.

That is the only path I will ever map here.

Same docket day as BPC-157. Same procedural framework. Different compound, different indication, different mechanism.

🧵 KPV going into the PCAC:

---

Background.

KPV is a short tripeptide fragment of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH). It has been studied for anti-inflammatory effects, primarily in murine models of inflammatory bowel disease.

The mechanism is well-characterized in animal literature. Human data is limited.

---

Regulatory state going in:

Like BPC-157, KPV was on the Category 2 bulk substances list and was removed in April 2026.

The Category 2 placement cited "significant safety risks" + insufficient characterization for human use — manufacturing and safety concerns, not efficacy findings.

---

What's actually being evaluated July 23:

The PCAC will review available data on KPV for wound healing and inflammatory conditions and vote on whether to recommend inclusion on the 503A Bulks List.

This is a procedural evaluation, not an approval hearing.

---

The non-binding nature matters here.

A PCAC "yes" is a recommendation. The FDA weighs it, may accept or reject it, and issues its own determination on 503A Bulks List inclusion.

If the FDA follows a positive recommendation, state-licensed 503A pharmacies could compound KPV under physician prescription. Nothing more.

---

What this would and would not change:

Would change: legal pathway for physician-supervised access via compounding pharmacies.

Would NOT change: FDA-approval status (still unapproved for any indication), direct-to-consumer legality (still illegal), gray-market sourcing (still illegal), and "research only" labeling that names human therapeutic uses (still misbranding under 21 CFR 201.128).

---

Inflammatory conditions are real and serious. The mechanisms KPV touches are well-described in the literature. None of that changes the legal architecture around access.

Physician-supervised, compounded, prescribed. That sequence exists for a reason. Skipping any step puts the entire operation in the FDA's enforcement lane.

The PCAC will review available data on MOTs-C for the obesity indication — metabolic regulation, body composition, weight-related outcomes.

Both votes are non-binding recommendations to the FDA. The agency then issues its own determination on 503A Bulks List inclusion — sometimes months later.

Animal data on MOTs-C and metabolic regulation is suggestive. Human data is limited.

What you can do as a reader: separate "the mechanism is interesting" from "this compound is approved for X." Those statements are years of regulatory work apart.
